examShortTricks: Trick 1: Hydrogen fuel merits in three points — high calorific value (~150 kJ/g), only product is water, no CO2/SO2 pollution; demerit: storage and production cost.
Trick 2: Heavy water D2O is made by repeated electrolysis of ordinary water (D2O is left behind); it is the MODERATOR and coolant in nuclear reactors — one line each for preparation and use.
Trick 3: D2O retards plant growth and kills germs at high concentration — the classic 'biological effect' 1-marker.
keyPoints: Hydrogen as fuel: high heat of combustion and pollution-free product (H2O).
Heavy water (D2O): deuterium oxide, prepared by prolonged electrolysis of water.
D2O is used as a moderator and coolant in nuclear reactors.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is hydrogen called a clean fuel? (1 mark) — burns to water only; no CO, CO2 or SO2.
Q. What is heavy water and one use? (2 marks) — D2O; moderator/coolant in nuclear reactors.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Define allotropy with two O examples (O2 dioxygen, O3 ozone) and two S examples (rhombic, monoclinic) — definition + examples earns both marks.
Trick 2: Oxide classification by reaction with water: acidic (non-metal oxides: CO2, SO2), basic (metal oxides: Na2O, CaO), amphoteric (both: Al2O3, ZnO), neutral (CO, N2O, NO).
Trick 3: Peroxides give H2O2 with water/acid (Na2O2, BaO2); higher oxides of Pb are oxidising — quote one equation to secure the mark.
keyPoints: Allotropy: existence of an element in two or more forms in the same physical state.
Oxides: acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral and peroxide types.
Acidic oxides come from non-metals; basic from metals; amphoteric react with both acids and bases.
practiceQuestions: Q. Classify CO2, CaO, Al2O3, CO by oxide type. (2 marks) — acidic; basic; amphoteric; neutral.
Q. Define allotropy with an example from oxygen. (1 mark) — O2 and O3 are allotropes of oxygen.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Preparation equation to memorise: 3O2 —(silent electric discharge)→ 2O3; 'silent discharge' and 'endothermic' are the scoring keywords.
Trick 2: Structure: bent molecule, bond angle ~117°, resonance between two O–O=O forms; average bond order 1.5 — draw the resonance pair.
Trick 3: Test: ozone turns starch–iodide paper blue (liberates I2 from KI); uses: sterilising water, bleaching oils, absorbing UV in the stratosphere.
keyPoints: Ozone occurs in the stratosphere (ozone layer) and is prepared from oxygen by silent electric discharge.
Bent triatomic molecule with resonance; bond angle about 117°.
Test: liberates iodine from KI (starch paper turns blue); used for water sterilisation and UV absorption.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the preparation of ozone with conditions. (2 marks) — 3O2 → 2O3 by silent electric discharge (endothermic).
Q. Give the test for ozone. (1 mark) — turns starch–iodide paper blue due to I2 liberation.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Colour-change table for the 3-mark answer — CuSO4: pale blue → deep blue (tetraammine complex); FeCl3: yellow → brown (Fe(OH)3); Hg2Cl2: black (amido-mercury).
Trick 2: With conc. HCl: white fumes of NH4Cl (fountain/fuming test); with water: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH− shows basic nature.
Trick 3: Always write NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl (white fumes) — it is both a property AND a test for ammonia.
keyPoints: NH3 with CuSO4: Cu(OH)2 precipitate dissolves in excess NH3 giving deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+.
NH3 with FeCl3 gives brown Fe(OH)3 precipitate.
NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl (dense white fumes).
Aqueous NH3 is weakly basic due to OH− formation.
practiceQuestions: Q. What happens when ammonia is passed into CuSO4 solution? (2 marks) — pale blue Cu(OH)2 then deep blue complex [Cu(NH3)4]SO4 in excess.
Q. Give one test to identify NH3 gas. (1 mark) — white fumes with conc. HCl (rod dipped in HCl).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Memorise the four: HNO2 nitrous (+3), HNO3 nitric (+5), H2N2O2 hyponitrous (+1), H4N2O4 hydronitrous... use the pair nitrous/nitric as the core answer and add HNO4 pernitric if asked for more.
Trick 2: Oxidation-state check earns the mark: N in HNO2 is +3, in HNO3 is +5 — show the arithmetic.
Trick 3: HNO2 disproportionates: 3HNO2 → HNO3 + 2NO + H2O — a favourite 1-marker.
keyPoints: Oxy-acids of nitrogen: hyponitrous H2N2O2, nitrous HNO2, nitric HNO3, pernitric HNO4.
Nitrogen oxidation states: +1, +3, +5 in the main oxy-acids.
HNO2 is unstable and disproportionates to HNO3 and NO.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name and give formulas of two oxy-acids of nitrogen. (2 marks) — nitrous acid HNO2, nitric acid HNO3.
Q. What is the oxidation state of N in HNO2? (1 mark) — +3.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Dilute HNO3 + metals → NO; conc. HNO3 + metals → NO2 — pick the gas by acid strength (except Mg with dilute gives H2, and Au/Pt dissolve in aqua regia only).
Trick 2: Passivity: cold conc. HNO3 makes Fe, Al, Cr passive (oxide film) — a guaranteed 1-marker.
Trick 3: Non-metals oxidised: S → H2SO4, P → H3PO4, C → CO2 — write one equation: C + 4HNO3 → CO2 + 4NO2 + 2H2O.
Trick 4: Brown-ring test for nitrate: FeSO4 + conc. H2SO4 gives a brown ring at the junction — the classic identification test.
keyPoints: HNO3 is both a strong acid and a strong oxidising agent.
With Cu: 3Cu + 8HNO3(dil) → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O; with conc.: NO2 evolves.
Fe, Al, Cr become passive in cold concentrated HNO3.
Oxidises S, P, C to their highest oxides/acids.
practiceQuestions: Q. Copper with dilute and concentrated HNO3 — write both equations. (3 marks) — dilute → NO; conc. → NO2 (Cu(NO3)2 + H2O co-products).
Q. Why is Al not attacked by cold conc. HNO3? (1 mark) — passivation by a protective oxide layer.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Trend line for the 3-mark answer: reactivity and oxidising power F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; b.p./m.p. and colour intensity increase DOWN the group.
Trick 2: Displacement series: F2 displaces all; Cl2 displaces Br− and I−; Br2 displaces I− only — write Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2.
Trick 3: Preparation: MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O (lab method); I2 from KI + oxidant — one equation each.
Trick 4: Why F2 is strongest oxidant: low bond dissociation energy + high hydration energy of F−.
keyPoints: Halogens: F2, Cl2, Br2, I2 — highly reactive non-metals with 7 valence electrons.
Oxidising power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
Cl2 prepared in the lab by heating MnO2 with concentrated HCl.
Higher halogens displace lower ones from their salts.
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange halogens by oxidising power and justify. (2 marks) — F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2; decreasing electrode potential down the group.
Q. Write the lab preparation of chlorine. (2 marks) — MnO2 + 4HCl(conc.) → MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O on heating.
